projects.name: Utooni Development Organisation
projects.intro:
Utooni Development Organization, is an NGO working in the arid and semi arid land (ASAL) areas of South Eastern Kenya. This presentation shares Utooni's work of enabling communities living in these ASAL areas to improve water security through construction of sand dams and shallow wells. The presentation discusses their viability, implementation, management, benefits and challenges.

Sand dams are concrete walls constructed along seasonal rivers to harvest and store water during the rainy season in order to provide communities with a reliable source of water during the dry season.

Shallow wells are constructed near sand dams (along seasonal rivers) to improve the quality of water and to make it easier for community members, especially women and girls to access water.

projects.name: SCOPE Kenya Water Harvesting in Schools
projects.intro:
John Macharia, the National Coordinator presents SCOPE Kenya's work. John focuses on water harvesting and management for enhanced land regeneration, and food production and biodiversity conservation among school communities.

We hear case studies of schools which have excelled well in putting up rain surface runoff management systems, resulting in reduced soil erosion, and increased regreening of their landscapes, with well-established food forest through permaculture approaches. Also, we will hear how this knowledge has been adopted by neighbouring community members, contributing to improved food security, livelihoods and environmental conservation.

projects.name: Practical Permaculture Institute Impact
projects.intro:
Josephat Barasa of Practical Permaculture Institute, along with colleague Walter Mugove show the impact of the water retaining structures on the farms, the landscapes and the communities. The presentation shows photos of Josephat's work in school gardens, farms of men and women farmers.

Some questions the presentation addresses: How does one scale out this work in water retention on farms and landscapes? What are the challenges encountered and how have they been overcome? How can smallholders farmers and children remain motivated to keep on working on water retention?

projects.name: Dabane Trust
projects.intro: Dabane Trust is a Non-Governmental organization founded in 1991 and registered in Zimbabwe. In this online Water School Africa meeting, they share 32 years' experience working in South and North Zimbabwe. Dabane Trust presents how they use participatory, community-led development approach integrated with technical expertise for protection and improvement of soil, water and vegetation resources in the watershed, including co-creation of watershed infrastructure.

projects.name: Zephaniah Phiri Legacy
projects.intro: A tribute to the life and work of Zephaniah Phiri, who was an inspiration to thousands of people in Zimbabwe and beyond. He understood water and the role of farmers in their relationship with water brilliantly. He applied this understanding in a very practical way on his own farm and also in urging others to put in their own water-harvesting systems. In this discussion forum of Water School Africa we watch and hear about both his water-harvesting systems and how he inspired so many others.

projects.name: Chikukwa Ecological Land Use Trust
projects.intro: Chikukwa Ecological Land Use Community Trust (CELUCT) is a community-based organization founded in 1991. CELUCT's purpose is to facilitate the regeneration of community cohesion and landscape through training programs, strengthening community relations, advocacy, research and critical awareness raising. They use different approaches according to a community's needs. In their presentation, CELUCT will share 30 years of experience working in Chikukwa communal land and beyond in Chimanimani district in Zimbabwe. At the heart of their work has been how to hold water in their landscapes. Given the topography of Chikukwa and the cyclones that inevitably arrive periodically, they have had no alternative but to focus on water. They have had many successes but also learnt from what has not gone so well.

projects.name: Muonde Trust
projects.intro:
The Muonde Trust is a community-based organisation in the dry, south-west of Zimbabwe. Community-driven water-harvesting is at the heart of their work. Their formation was inspired by the work of Zimbabwe's Waterman, Zephaniah Phiri, who spent some years working in Mazvihwa in the 1980s, with those who later formed the Muonde Trust.

Well worth watching for anyone interested in this kind of grounded holding-water-in-the-landscape work. Members of Muonde Trust now have years of experience, which comes through in their presentation and in the Q and A session which followed.

projects.name: Zimsoff Shashe Case Study
projects.intro:
Nelson Mudzingwa of Shashe Block of Farms, Zimbabwe, presents his experiences of restoring the water cycle through traditional methods of earth dams, dead level contours and stone barriers/ walls, and interlocked keyhole beds as part of a social, ecological and agricultural transformation.

Everything in Nelson's story from the collapse to the regeneration with the community of the water cycle, is told through the simple observation of nature and the experience of doing the work. It highlights what can happen when the collaboration of local communities and their knowledge, wisdom and successes are shared widely.

projects.name: Groundswell International and Terre Verte
projects.intro:
Groundswell West Africa is a partnership in four countries in West Africa – Mali, Burkina Faso, Senegal and Ghana. Much of their work happens in the Sahel region where every drop of rain counts so over the years various practices have been developed by farmers and communities in the region to hold more water in their landscapes. Tsuamba Bourgou will share some of those experiences. He will also introduce the work of Terre Verte, a partner organisation working in the Sahel.

Tsuamba Bourgou is Groundswell's Regional Coordinator for West Africa. He lives in Fada N'Gourma, Burkina Faso. Tsuamba's areas of experience include adult education, action research, evaluation, impact assessment, strategic planning and facilitation and local capacity building. He holds a Master degree in linguistics from the University of Ouagadougou. Tsuamba is a keen and practicing farmer, producing real food for his own household and local markets, using agroecological practices.

projects.name: Tiyeni
projects.intro: Mr Isaac Monjo Chavula, an Executive Director of Tiyeni, Malawi, introduces us to a pioneering method called Deep Bed Farming (DBF) which they have developed over several years of trial and error working with farmers and communities in Malawi . DBF involves breaking up hard compacted layers of earth several inches under the ground, which allows roots, water and air to penetrate more deeply underground, and helps the soil retain water and moisture long after the rains, instead of running off immediately after rainfall and causing devastating soil erosion.

projects.name: Wisdom and renewal of Nile water culture
projects.intro:
During the session of the Water School Africa, Nourane Amr of Nile Journeys (Nurturing Impulses for Living Ecosystems: NILE) describes her partnership with the local communities along the Nile Valley tapping into very ancient wisdom and know-how to illustrate how good environmental practices and effective water harvesting can enhance community sustainability. The word “NILE” in NILE Journeys represents more than just the Nile River; it symbolizes the energetic essence of this majestic waterway.

Nourane Amr explores one of the 21 project prototypes catalyzed by them, which are implemented in Heissa Island, near Aswan, Egypt, a serene gem of Nubian culture and history and is one of the last remaining Nubian islands, having survived the challenges of flooding caused by the construction of the reservoir dam.

Discover the untapped resilience of this community, standing strong through generations despite the challenges of the reservoir and dam construction.

projects.name: Effective Watershed Reclamation by Communities in Cameroon
projects.intro:
Eric Wirsiy from CENDEP, Cameroon explores the impact of forest destruction on water availability. Massive forest areas have been destroyed in the name of development and farming activities, leaving communities without sufficient water for its requirements.

In Northwestern Cameroon, the community of Mbiame, with support from CENDEP, has restored a degraded forest through a massive reforestation program covering an area of over 1050 hectares.

The presentation communicates an inspiring and successful story of watershed reclamation and its impact on improving water availability locally.

projects.name: Water Harvesting in Rwanda
projects.intro:
The INGABO syndicate is a network of over 16,000 farmers, 54.1% of which are women spread across 10 provinces in Rwanda. Recognized by the government in 2005, it promotes different sustainable water harvesting techniques. The INGABO syndicate also encourages different traditional methods to retain moisture and sustain food cropping. This syndicate is a member of the East Africa Farmers Federation and the World Farmers Organization.

In this session our hosts from INGABO syndicate are the CEO Mbabazi Fracois Xavier, Senior Agronomist Manariyo Victor, Communication Officer Byiringiro Jean Paul and Session presenter Agronomist Dutonnyekumana Prosper together with community farmers picked around the 10 provinces of Rwanda. We learn from the farmers who are transforming their lives through sustainable water harvesting how the syndicate empowers communities through training in water retention to alleviate hunger and poverty.

projects.name: WSI Khajuaraho
projects.intro:
The visionary head of Parmarth Social Service Organisation, Mr Sanjay Singh talks about the models they have created for women to take the lead in reviving their water sources as well as the innovative governance models they have initiated at a village level. Sanjay Singh also talks about the setting up of the Water School India in collaboration with the Flow Partnership UK.

Sanjay Singh is joined by some of the Jal Sahelis, (Friends of Water) who are a growing group of women responsible for creating awareness amongst their communities on water rights. They also mobilize their communities to participate in resolving village water issues and in preparing a water user master plan for their villages. Jal Sahelis give solutions to all kinds of problems related to water to the people of their villages including on water harvesting, water conservation, deepening of wells, rehabilitation of water structures, building small dams, repairing hand pumps and getting community participation with the government on its water revival schemes.

Sanjay Singh has done pioneering work in the field of water conservation in the historically drought-prone and extremely backward region of Bundelkhand in Uttar Pradesh, India over the last 27 years through his NGO Parmarth Social Service Organisation. He is also affectionately called the Waterman of Bundelkhand.

projects.name: Belford
projects.intro:
Dr Paul Quinn, a pioneering hydrologist presents his field work, GIS and modelling methods to address water-based issues. With his colleagues he has developed the concept of catchment systems engineering. Working with stakeholders, policy makers and industry, they are now engineering solutions to water quantity and quality issues, by building bunds, wetlands and ponds on farms and in forests.

Our landscape is now malfunctioning, and the climate is changing so we must manage the water once it falls from the sky. We have too much runoff and not enough water in the soil and rocks. We should lower floods, droughts and erosion. Runoff Attenuation Features are small, engineered features to slow and store water in the landscape.

Paul shows a number of case studies and the lessons they have learned so far and the evidence they have for changing the whole landscape whilst still producing food and trees.

Paul Quinn is also a Senior Scientist at the James Hutton Institute/Scotland; a Visiting Fellow Newcastle University/UK as well as at Trinity College Dublin/Ireland.

projects.name: People and Water
projects.intro:
Michal Kravcik and Danka Kravcikova of People and Water Solvakia have developed far reaching tools to estimate the run off of water in a region and to implement measures to hold the water in the ground.

One way of slowing the rain so it can sink into the ground is to build log dams higher up the catchment, in the forest, which will impede the run off from storm events, allow infiltration and distribute the water into the wider landscape.

The footage is filmed from the building of a leaky wooden dam at a Summer School event in 2019, attended by the Flow Partnership

projects.name: Water School South America
projects.intro:
Water School South America began with a promise from the children of Barichara, Colombia. Their parents contacted The Flow Partnership in 2021 with tales of dry tributaries in Barichara, wondering what they could do and how they might involve their community in regeneration to become water secure.

From then on, a ground movement of traditional water retention practices, modern successful techniques and intervention, has brought the local mayors and politicians on side. A whole host of concerned and willing folk in the local communities in Colombia and in the other countries have been coming together and setting up a system of learning and implementation with the Flow Partnership’s Water Schools, that will be culturally relevant and impactful across the continent.

Water School South America is launching as a water literacy, knowledge exchange, and seed-dispersion platform for community-led restoration in the region.

It will stimulate decentralized action by from concept to demonstration and then realisation. It will link the methodology of the global Water Schools platform to inspire other communities with online presentations of successful methods and stimulate decentralized water activation through mechanisms such as the “Water Cup” challenge—an incentive-based mechanism for communities to implement water retention practices using their own initiative and resources.

It will also continuously facilitate South–South learning exchanges with practitioners from Water School India and Africa.

More soon…
